title: Transactions & Isolation
subtitle: Watch two concurrent transactions corrupt a bank balance, then see how logs, row versions, and locks stop it.
learn: What each letter of ACID promises, and which part of the engine delivers it
How lost updates, dirty reads, and write skew actually happen
How MVCC lets readers and writers work without blocking each other
When to reach for row locks, SELECT FOR UPDATE, or serializable isolation
Why stronger isolation costs waiting or retries

steps.title: Two people, one balance
steps.body: An account holds $100. Transaction A and Transaction B each want to withdraw $30 at the same moment, perhaps from two phones. The right final balance is $40. A database serving thousands of such requests per second must get that right every time, even when requests overlap or the machine dies mid-way. A transaction is the tool for this: a group of reads and writes treated as one unit.
steps.idea: A transaction groups several operations into one all-or-nothing unit, and the database must keep concurrent units from corrupting each other.
steps.caption: Two transactions about to touch the same $100 row.

steps.title: All or nothing
steps.body: A transfer debits one account and credits another. If the server crashes between the two writes, money vanishes. Atomicity says both happen or neither does. The engine first appends every change to a write-ahead log (WAL), a sequential file, tagged with the transaction id. On a crash it replays or undoes from that log, so a half-finished transaction never survives restart.
steps.idea: Atomicity comes from logging changes first, so an unfinished transaction can always be rolled back.
steps.caption: Changes are logged before they count.

steps.title: Commit means it stays
steps.body: When A sends COMMIT, the engine forces the log to disk (an fsync) and only then answers success. On a typical NVMe SSD that costs well under a millisecond; on a network disk, a few milliseconds. Durability means a committed transaction survives a power cut. Consistency, the C in ACID, means your rules (no negative balance, foreign keys) hold before and after; the database enforces declared constraints, but your code defines the rest.
steps.idea: Durability means the commit record is on disk before the client hears 'committed'.
steps.caption: Commit waits for the log to reach disk.

steps.title: Lost update
steps.body: Now the overlap. Both transactions read the balance (100) into the application, subtract 30 in code, and write back 70. A writes 70, then B writes 70. Each transaction looked fine on its own, but one withdrawal vanished: the balance should be 40. This is a lost update, and it is the classic bug of read-modify-write done in application code without protection.
steps.idea: A lost update happens when two transactions read the same old value and the later write overwrites the earlier one.
steps.caption: Both read 100, both write 70.

steps.title: Dirty read
steps.body: A different problem: A writes 70 but has not committed yet. If B is allowed to read that uncommitted 70 and acts on it, and then A rolls back, B used a number that never officially existed. That is a dirty read. The Read Committed isolation level (the default in PostgreSQL and many others) forbids it: you only ever see data from transactions that have committed.
steps.idea: Isolation levels are promises about which anomalies you can never see; Read Committed rules out dirty reads.
steps.caption: B sees A's uncommitted write, then A rolls back.

steps.title: Keep old versions around
steps.body: Instead of blocking readers while A writes, most modern engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle) use multi-version concurrency control. A write creates a new version of the row and keeps the old one. Each transaction reads from a snapshot, so B keeps seeing 100 until A commits. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers. The price is storage for old versions and cleanup later (VACUUM in PostgreSQL).
steps.idea: MVCC gives each transaction a consistent snapshot by keeping old row versions, so reads do not wait for writes.
steps.caption: B reads the old version while A's new one is pending.

steps.title: Make B wait its turn
steps.body: Snapshots stop dirty reads but not lost updates in app code. The fix is to lock the row you intend to change: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE. A gets the row lock first. B asks for the same lock and is made to wait. When A commits, B's read returns 70, and B writes 40. B waited, say 12 ms, but the answer is correct. Often you can skip all this with a single statement: UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - 30.
steps.idea: Row locks serialize writers on the same row: correctness is bought with waiting.
steps.caption: B blocks on A's row lock, then sees 70.

steps.title: Write skew
steps.body: Locks on one row do not help when two transactions write different rows based on a shared rule. Say checking and savings hold $60 each, and the rule is that the total must stay at or above 0. A withdraws $100 from checking, B withdraws $100 from savings. Each checks the total (120), sees room, and writes a different row. Snapshot isolation sees no conflict, so both commit and the total is -80.
steps.idea: Write skew breaks a rule spanning several rows even though no single row was written twice.
steps.caption: Different rows, shared rule, both commit.

steps.title: Serializable and its price
steps.body: Serializable isolation promises results as if transactions ran one at a time. PostgreSQL does this by tracking which rows each transaction read and wrote; if it spots a dangerous pattern, one transaction is aborted with a serialization error, and the app must retry. Other engines use more locking and more waiting. Safety rises along Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable, and so does the cost, so many teams stay at a lower level and protect only the risky paths.
steps.idea: Stronger isolation trades throughput for safety: more waiting, or more aborted transactions to retry.
steps.caption: The engine aborts B; the app retries and sees -40 is not allowed.

steps.title: Pick the weakest safe tool
steps.body: ACID: atomic via the log, consistent via your rules, isolated via MVCC and locks, durable via fsync on commit. Lost updates call for atomic UPDATEs or FOR UPDATE; dirty reads are gone at Read Committed; write skew needs Serializable or an explicit lock on a shared row. Keep transactions short, always retry on serialization or deadlock errors, and never hold one open across a user click. Spanning several databases needs more machinery, covered in later lessons.
steps.idea: Use the cheapest mechanism that rules out the anomaly you actually risk, and always be ready to retry.
steps.caption: Log, versions, and locks each cover a different failure.

quiz.q: Two requests each run SELECT balance, compute balance - 30 in app code, then UPDATE with the computed value. Both read 100. What final balance results at Read Committed with no locks?
options: 40, because the database serializes the updates
70, because the second write overwrites the first
100, because both transactions roll back
The second transaction always gets an error
quiz.why: Read Committed does not stop two transactions reading the same old value. The later write of 70 overwrites the earlier one, a lost update.

quiz.q: Why does MVCC let a long report query run while writers keep updating the same table?
options: Writers are paused until the report ends
The report reads a snapshot made of older row versions, so it does not need locks held by writers
The report reads uncommitted data
The report runs on the write-ahead log
quiz.why: MVCC keeps old versions, so the reader sees a consistent snapshot while writers create new versions. Neither blocks the other.

quiz.q: On-call rule: at least one doctor must stay on call. Two doctors, both on call, each check the count (2) and then set only their own row to off. Both commit under snapshot isolation. What happened?
options: A dirty read
A lost update
Write skew
A deadlock
quiz.why: They wrote different rows, so there was no write-write conflict, yet the shared rule broke. That is write skew, prevented by Serializable or a lock on a shared row.

quiz.q: Your service runs at Serializable isolation and sometimes gets a serialization error on commit. What is the correct response?
options: Treat it as a bug and lower the isolation level silently
Ignore it, the data is already saved
Rerun the whole transaction from the start, usually with a small retry limit
Retry only the last statement
quiz.why: A serialization failure means the transaction was aborted to keep results correct. The whole transaction must be retried, since its earlier reads may now be stale.

quiz.q: What does the write-ahead log mainly provide?
options: Faster reads through caching
Atomic rollback and durable commits after a crash
Protection against write skew
Automatic sharding
quiz.why: Logging changes before applying them lets the engine undo unfinished transactions and replay committed ones after a crash.

cheatsheet.def: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes).
Reading another transaction's uncommitted data, which may later be rolled back. Prevented from Read Committed upward.
Two read-modify-write cycles overlap and one overwrites the other. Fix with atomic UPDATE, SELECT FOR UPDATE, or version checks.
Two transactions read overlapping data, write different rows, and together break a rule. Needs Serializable or an explicit shared lock.
Multi-version concurrency control: writes add row versions and reads use snapshots, so readers and writers rarely block each other.
Read Committed (default in PostgreSQL), Repeatable Read (default in MySQL InnoDB), Serializable. Exact guarantees vary by engine, so check yours.
Reads rows and locks them until commit, so concurrent writers wait. Keep the transaction short to limit waiting and deadlocks.
Serialization failures and deadlocks are normal under contention. Rerun the whole transaction, with a cap and a little jitter.
